title: Germany and Russia Hold Rare Talks at U.N., but Tensions Remain
summary:
The top diplomats of Germany and Russia met face-to-face on Saturday for what is believed to be the first such meeting since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The roughly 20-minute meeting, held on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, ended with a handshake — but little agreement.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul requested the meeting and called on Russia to abandon its "dangerous path of escalation" toward Germany, Europe and the NATO alliance, according to a German delegation official. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was dismissive. At a news conference afterward, he said "nothing new" came from the conversation.

Lavrov then took the rostrum at the General Assembly, where he accused Germany of being Ukraine's main sponsor and seeking to become a leading military power in Europe. "Does Berlin understand what this could lead to?" he asked. "Didn't they not learn the lessons of World War II?" He also criticized the militarization of Japan and made clear Russia will veto any attempt by Germany or Japan to gain permanent seats on the U.N. Security Council — the U.N.'s most powerful body. The United States has long supported permanent seats for those countries and India.

Ties between Russia and Germany have soured in recent weeks, following an attempted drone attack last month at Leipzig airport, which Germany blames on Russia, and tit-for-tat responses.

Lavrov defended Russia's war in Ukraine and criticized the West for trying to "impose its own rules on everyone else," saying a "fairer, multipolar world order is emerging." Wadephul, in his own U.N. address, said "Russia's war targets the lives of millions of innocent people" and urged Russia to negotiate an end to the fighting.

The war has killed or wounded hundreds of thousands of soldiers on both sides, according to Western estimates, and disrupted global fuel, fertilizer and grain shipments. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pressed allies on Saturday to keep choking Russia's revenues, writing, "Russia is escalating every single day."
why_it_matters: This meeting shows both the value and the limits of diplomacy: talking can keep channels open, but when one side's veto power and the other side's sanctions meet, ordinary people far from the table still face higher fuel, fertilizer and food prices, and the war grinds on.

background_read: The U.N. General Assembly (the yearly gathering in New York where leaders and diplomats from nearly every country give speeches) has long been a stage for rivalries as much as for cooperation.

Germany and Russia have a complicated history — Germany was split in two during the Cold War — and modern Germany has become one of Ukraine's biggest military and financial backers since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, which is why Moscow now attacks Berlin rather than treats it as a partner.

NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance of the United States, Canada and most European countries) has expanded eastward since the 1990s, something Moscow has repeatedly called a security threat.

The U.N. Security Council (the body that can impose sanctions or authorize military force) has five permanent members — the U.S., Russia, China, the U.K. and France — each holding a veto; Germany, Japan, India and Brazil have pushed for permanent seats for years, so Russia's promise to veto those bids shows how hard reform is.

Lavrov's talk of a 'multipolar' order reflects Russia's argument that the era of one superpower writing the rules is over, while Western officials say Moscow simply wants a free hand to attack its neighbours.

perspectives.description: Even a 20-minute meeting and a handshake keep a channel open between two governments that have barely spoken since 2022, and Germany's push for U.N. Security Council reform keeps a long-stalled debate alive.
Lavrov dismissed the conversation outright and used the U.N. stage to accuse Germany of fuelling the war, so critics argue the meeting gave Moscow a platform rather than a reason to change course.

Russia presents itself as the leader of a 'multipolar' world challenging Western dominance, while Germany invokes the lessons of World War II — two very different readings of history colliding inside the same building.

The real test is whether quieter back-channel contacts survive the public insults, and whether Western pressure on Russian oil and gas revenue — the tactic Zelenskyy is urging allies to intensify — actually shifts Moscow's calculations.
